---
title: "Verify before you commit, and let GitHub verify too"
---

Your bracelet project has tests now, and `npm run verify` still knows nothing
about them. This chapter puts the test run into that one command, and then
hands the command to a computer at GitHub that runs it after every push and
marks the commit green or red.

## Three checks in one command {#sec-verify-ci-experiment}

Open `homework/bracelet-tests` and find the `verify` line in `package.json`.
You have added it to every project since the chapter on scripts and assets:

```json
"verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check ."
```

Put the test run at the end of it:

```json
"verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check . && vitest run"
```

Run it:

```bash
npm run verify
```

```
> startercode@1.0.0 verify
> tsc --noEmit && biome check . && vitest run

Checked 18 files in 5ms. No fixes applied.

 RUN  v4.1.11 .../homework/bracelet-tests

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

Your project prints its own file count and test count. The line calls
`vitest run` and not `npm test`, because `npm test` would only start another
npm script that runs the same thing.

Now break something. Open `src/bracelet.test.ts`, pick a test that counts
items, and change the expected number to a wrong one. Run `npm run verify`
again:

```
Checked 18 files in 5ms. No fixes applied.

 ❯ src/bracelet.test.ts (8 tests | 1 failed) 9ms
     × holds two items after a letter and a spacer 5ms

⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Tests 1 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

 FAIL  src/bracelet.test.ts > Bracelet > holds two items after a letter and a spacer
AssertionError: expected [ LetterCube{ letter: 'A' }, …(1) ] to have a length of 3 but got 2

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 7 passed (8)
```

Your own test name stands in the `FAIL` line, and under it Vitest prints the
same failure report you read in the Vitest chapter, shortened here. The type
check and Biome both ran and said nothing, and the run stopped red on the
tests.

Break it harder. In the same test file, write `bracelet.addLetter(1);` inside
one of the tests, with a number where a letter belongs. Run `npm run verify`
once more:

```
> startercode@1.0.0 verify
> tsc --noEmit && biome check . && vitest run

src/bracelet.test.ts(17,24): error TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'.
```

That is the whole output. Biome and Vitest never ran, so the wrong number in
the test is still waiting for you: `&&` starts the next command only when the
one before it succeeded. Undo both changes and run `npm run verify` until it is
green again.

## What the chain is for {#sec-verify-ci-chain}

One command answers one question: is this project in a state you can hand in?
The type check comes first because its errors make the other two pointless: a
test that does not compile proves nothing. The tests come last because they
are the slowest, and a run that stops earlier saves you the wait. Green before
every commit stays the rule.

## A computer that is not yours {#sec-verify-ci-what}

Running `verify` yourself has one hole in it: it checks the files on your disk,
and what your teacher reads is the repository on GitHub. A file you forgot to
commit is on your disk and not in the repository, and a package you installed
by hand months ago is not in `package.json` either. Both make your laptop say
green and everybody else's computer say red.

**Continuous integration** closes that hole. Every time you push, GitHub starts
a fresh computer, downloads what is in your repository, installs the packages
the project asks for, and runs your `verify`. The commit gets a yellow dot
while the run is going, then a green check mark or a red cross. People shorten
continuous integration to CI, and you will see the two letters everywhere.
Nobody has to remember to start it, which is what makes the file below worth
writing once.

## The workflow file {#sec-verify-ci-workflow}

GitHub reads its instructions from a file in your repository, and the file is
written in YAML. YAML is another way to write the kind of data you know from
`package.json`, with indentation in place of the curly braces and a `-` in
front of every item of a list. Indentation carries meaning here, so spaces
matter and tabs are forbidden.

This is the whole file. It goes into the **root of your `creative-coding-2`
repository**, in `.github/workflows/verify.yml`, not into the project folder:

```yaml
name: Verify
on: [push]

jobs:
  bracelet-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: homework/bracelet-tests
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: homework/bracelet-tests/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run verify
```

`name: Verify` is the title of the workflow in the Actions tab, and it is yours
to choose. `on: [push]` lists the events that start it, and GitHub's
documentation lists the other events you could put in that list.

`jobs:` opens the list of jobs, and `bracelet-tests:` is the name of the single
job here. A job is one machine working through one sequence of steps.

`runs-on: ubuntu-latest` picks that machine. GitHub hands you a fresh Linux
computer and throws it away when the run ends, so nothing from one run can leak
into the next.

`defaults: run: working-directory:` says where every `run:` step starts.
Without it `npm ci` would start in the repository root, where there is no
project at all.

`steps:` is the sequence, top to bottom. A step with `uses:` runs a ready-made
action that somebody else published, named `owner/name@version`. A step with
`run:` runs a shell command, the same one you type in your own terminal.

`actions/checkout@v7` downloads your repository onto the machine, which is
empty without it. `actions/setup-node@v7` installs Node, and its three settings
pick the version and keep the downloaded packages of that one project between
runs, so later runs start faster.

`npm ci` installs the packages. It is the install command made for machines
like this one: it installs the exact versions your project recorded instead of
looking for newer ones, so a run today and a run in March test the same code
with the same packages.

`npm run verify` is your own command, the one you just extended. Everything
above exists to get to this line, and two of those lines name your project
folder. Yours probably starts with the lesson date, the way the git chapter
set up your repository, so write your own folder name in both places.

::: {.research title="What is actually running your tests?"}
The exercise below pushes this file and reads a red run, and three pieces of
that are not explained above. GitHub's pages about GitHub-hosted runners and
about workflow runs answer two, and the npm documentation for `npm ci` answers
the third.

1. `ubuntu-latest` is a machine GitHub starts for you. Which Ubuntu version
   does that name point to right now, and name two tools that are already
   installed on it before your first step runs. Say where you read it.
2. `npm ci` needs one file in the repository that `npm install` can live
   without. Which file is it, and what does `npm ci` do with a `node_modules`
   folder that is already there? Say where you read it.
3. A run went red. Describe the way from your repository page to the text
   output of the step that failed, and say what you click on the way.

For the exam, remember what `npm ci` needs. A project you hand in without that
file does not build anywhere but on your own laptop.
:::

## The rule your buddy follows {#sec-verify-ci-agents}

Your coding buddy can run commands, and `AGENTS.md` is where you tell it which
ones matter. Open `AGENTS.md` in `homework/bracelet-tests`, or create it when
the project has none yet, and make sure this line is in it, in your own words:

> Run `npm run verify` before you report that you are done, and fix everything
> it finds.

The sentence carries more weight than it did in the SVG part, because `verify`
now runs the tests. An agent that reports success tells you nothing you can check. One that
pastes the counts from its own `verify` run hands you the evidence with the
code.

Agents skip rules sometimes. When yours reports it is done without a `verify`
run, name the rule, and it runs the command.

## Exercise: CI for the bracelet project {#sec-verify-ci-exercise}

Your repository gets its first workflow, and you make it go red on purpose,
because a check you have never seen fail is a check you do not trust yet.

1. In the root of your `creative-coding-2` repository, put the workflow file
   from this chapter into `.github/workflows/verify.yml`, creating both folders
   on the way. Check that the two paths inside the file match your bracelet
   project's folder.

2. Make sure `homework/bracelet-tests/package.json` carries the extended
   `verify` line and that `npm run verify` is green in your terminal.

3. Commit both files and push. Expected result: a yellow dot next to your
   commit message on the repository page, and a green check mark a minute or
   two later.

4. Open the **Actions** tab, click the run, then the job, and find the output
   of `npm run verify`. Expected result: the same lines your own terminal
   printed, tests included. If the run stops at `npm ci` instead, your second
   research answer names the file that is missing from the repository, so add
   it and push again.

5. Break a test on purpose, exactly as you did in the experiment, then commit
   and push. Expected result: a red cross next to the commit. GitHub also sends
   you an email about a failed run of your own, unless you switched those
   emails off.

6. Open the red run and find the name of the failing test in the log, the way
   your third research answer describes. Then fix the test, push, and watch the
   commit turn green.

7. Add the `verify` rule to `AGENTS.md` if it is not there yet, then start `pi`
   in the project and ask it: *Add a test that removeLast twice on a bracelet
   with two items leaves it empty.* Read the test the agent wrote and
   decide whether it checks what you asked for. Expected result: the agent runs
   `npm run verify` on its own and reports what it printed. If it does not,
   tell it to.

8. Commit the new test together with `AGENTS.md`, and push. Expected result:
   green again, with one test more in the log than in step 4.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early: a second project

One job checks one project. Copy the whole `bracelet-tests:` block, name the
copy `travel-tests:`, and point its two paths at your travel costs project. The
two jobs run side by side on two machines, and the Actions tab shows two lines
per push. Push a broken travel project and watch one line go red while the
other stays green.
:::
